feedback: If the learner predicts a straight trace, or a curve 'because a force bends it': point out that no sideways push is applied — the disc or globe rotates beneath the straight-moving pen, so the trace curves.
If the learner cannot say why the hemispheres differ: have them view the spin from above each pole and notice the rotation appears opposite, which flips the apparent deflection.
activities.intendedInsight: Circulation wraps a rotating sphere; seeing a straight-intended path curve on a surface you can spin makes the apparent (frame-dependent) nature of Coriolis concrete, and the opposite deflection in each hemisphere follows from the direction of rotation seen from each pole.
learnerActions: On a spinnable 3D globe, launch a 'straight' path from the equator toward a pole and watch the trace curve relative to the rotating surface: in both hemispheres, a parcel moving toward the pole arcs eastward. On a physical turntable/lazy-Susan, which stands for one hemisphere seen from above its pole, draw a straight line with a pen across the spinning disc and watch the trace curve.
Compare launches in the Northern Hemisphere (path curves right) and the Southern Hemisphere (path curves left), and say why the two differ.
Peel back or tilt to view the three cells as latitude bands girdling the planet, and view the jet stream as a meandering ribbon from a polar vantage.
activities.title: Spin a globe and launch parcels across it (spatial Coriolis)

feedback: If a learner names a wind for where it blows TO: remind them winds are named for the direction they come FROM — a 'westerly' blows from the west.
If a learner says the equator is hottest because it is nearer the Sun: refocus on the angle of incidence — direct rays concentrate energy over a smaller area.
If a learner treats deserts as randomly placed hot spots: trace them to descending dry air in the subtropical high-pressure belts at ~30°.
If a learner cannot say why UK/US weather tends to arrive from the west: link it to the prevailing mid-latitude westerlies, which blow from west to east.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the discriminations after exploring the model: naming cells and belts, predicting deflection direction, locating deserts/rainforests from the circulation, and linking the westerlies to west-to-east weather turn the model into reliable, transferable knowledge.
learnerActions: Match each cell to its latitude band (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°) and each surface belt to its wind direction (trade winds easterly/equatorward, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies).
Sequence the causal chain: equator heated most → air rises → drifts poleward → sinks near 30° → returns as surface wind belt.
Given a poleward-launched parcel, draw or select its correctly curved path in each hemisphere (right in N, left in S).
Categorise named regions as wet-equatorial (rising air) or dry-subtropical (descending air at ~30°), e.g. placing the Sahara and Australian deserts under descending air.
Explain in your own words why the equator is hottest — sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating energy over less area — rather than because it is closer to the Sun.
Connect the mid-latitude westerlies to everyday experience: because they blow from the west, weather systems in the UK and US generally move from west to east.
activities.title: Consolidate: match, sequence, predict, and locate

feedback: If the learner invokes a sideways force: steer back to the rotating-frame account — the air moves nearly straight while the ground turns beneath it.

If the learner cites the plughole myth: note that at that scale the basin's shape and any leftover swirl in the water decide the spin direction; Coriolis matters only over large distances and long times.

If the learner says winds blow straight from high pressure to low pressure: the pressure difference starts the flow, but for large-scale winds rotation then curves it, so they do not travel in a straight line from high to low pressure. Near the equator and in small local winds such as sea breezes, this curving is weak.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the explanation aloud and responding to follow-up questions can expose and help repair the Coriolis-as-force and winds-named-from misconceptions that a diagram may leave hidden.
learnerActions: Pose and discuss whether the Coriolis effect is a real push on the air, and explain in your own words what actually makes a north-bound wind veer right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Ask why 'a westerly' is named for where the wind comes from, and check the drain/toilet-spin claim against the fact that Coriolis is negligible at small scales.
activities.title: Ask the meteorologist: untangle Coriolis and wind-naming
